========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, doctor, it's... it's a bit hard to explain, but I suppose the main reason I finally made this appointment—and my family has been telling me I need to talk to someone for a while now—is just this awful, constant feeling I have. I came in because I feel like I just cannot settle inside my own skin anymore. 

It's like... well, you know, at my age, I’m not working anymore, I'm supposed to be taking it easy, right? I should be sitting in my armchair, watching my daytime programs, maybe doing a crossword puzzle or just enjoying my retirement. But I can't. I absolutely cannot sit still. Just yesterday, I sat down because my back was aching and I was just so worn out. Completely exhausted to the bone. But the very second I sat down, it was like a motor switched on inside my chest. I had this overwhelming urge where I just have to jump right back up and do the next thing. 

I'll think, "Oh, I need to wipe down the kitchen counters," or "I should go reorganize the hall closet." And I don't even care about the closet! But it's this constant, buzzing need to just get up and move, even when I am so physically tired I could cry and I know I should just be sitting still. It's exhausting, it really is. I try to tell people it's like having bees in my veins, just pushing me to go, go, go, and I just want to rest. I really do want to rest, but my body just won't let me just be at peace for even five minutes...

Constantly worrying? Oh, well... no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I worry the normal amount, I think. Like, when my grandson got his driver's license last month, of course I worried! He's a good boy, but you know how teenagers are, and people drive like absolute maniacs on the highway these days. But it's not like I'm sitting around making up things to fret about, if that's what you mean. I don't lay awake at night terrified the house is going to catch fire or that the stock market is going to crash and take my little pension with it. My friend Barbara, now she's a worrier. She watches the news all day and gets herself into such a state about politics and the economy and everything else under the sun. I tell her, "Barb, turn off the television and go for a walk, you're making yourself sick!" 

So no, my mind isn't spinning with all these terrible thoughts or anything like that. It's really just my body that won't cooperate. My brain is perfectly fine just wanting to watch my shows or read a magazine, but my arms and legs and chest just have this... this frantic energy. It's not because I'm anxious about something bad happening, it's just that I physically cannot stay put. I just want to sit in my chair, but my body says, "No, get up, go do something, anything!" It's so frustrating, but no, it's not worry. It's just this awful restlessness.

Hot? Oh, no, I wouldn't say that. If anything, I'm the one who's always carrying a little cardigan around with me everywhere I go! I've been well past the menopause for years now, thank heavens, so those awful hot flashes are a thing of the past. So no, temperature-wise, my body is completely fine. Worse in the evening? You know, that's an interesting question. Let me think about that for a second. I mean, it's always there, this feeling like I just can't settle, but... no, I wouldn't say it's specifically worse at night. It's really just a constant thing, from the minute I wake up until I finally manage to exhaust myself enough to fall asleep. 

Actually, if I really think about it, my mornings might even be the most frantic time! I get up, usually around six—I've always been an early riser, Frank used to say I was up with the chickens—and the minute my feet hit the floor, it's like a motor starts running. I have to make the coffee, wipe down the counters, check the mail even though the mail carrier hasn't been there yet, water the African violets... it's just go, go, go. 

By the time the evening rolls around, I'm just so terribly tired from all the moving all day. I'll sit in my recliner—it's this lovely blue one I got on sale at Macy's three years ago, very comfortable—and I'll turn on Jeopardy, and I just want to sit there and watch it. But even then, my foot will be tapping, or I'll be picking at a loose thread on the armrest, or I'll suddenly feel the absolute need to get up and reorganize the magazine rack. 

So it's not that the urge to move gets *stronger* at night, it's just that I notice it more because that's when I'm actually trying to relax, if that makes sense. During the day, I can disguise it by doing chores, but at night, when I'm supposed to be resting, it just feels so much more... obvious, I guess. But the actual feeling, that buzzing, restless need to be doing something? No, that's pretty much the same level of awful all day long. It doesn't ramp up when the sun goes down or anything like that. It's just always there, driving me up the wall!

Relief? Oh, I don't know... not really. I mean, you'd think so, wouldn't you? You'd think if your body is screaming at you to get up and do something, doing it would make the feeling go away. But it doesn't, not really. 

Like yesterday, I was trying to sit and watch my shows—I like to watch the Wheel of Fortune right after Jeopardy, it's a nice little routine I've had for years—and I just couldn't do it. My legs felt like they had electricity running through them. So I got up and I started dusting the living room. I dusted the mantelpiece, I dusted the little porcelain figurines I collect—I have this lovely set of little dogs that Frank bought me for our anniversary one year, all different breeds, they're so sweet but they gather dust like you wouldn't believe. 

Anyway, I'm dusting, and I'm moving around, and sure, while I'm actually moving, I'm distracted. I'm focused on getting the dust off the little poodle's ears. But the minute I stop? The minute I put the duster away and try to go back to my chair? It's right back again. Instantly. It's not like scratching an itch where it feels better afterward. It's more like... like trying to empty the ocean with a teacup. You can keep scooping and scooping and moving and moving, but the water is still there. 

So I end up just pacing around the house, going from room to room, picking things up and putting them down, because stopping is just too uncomfortable. I'll walk into the kitchen to check the refrigerator, even though I just ate, and then I'll walk into the bedroom to smooth out the quilt, and then back to the living room. It's exhausting, it really is. I just wear myself out. But the restless feeling itself? No, moving doesn't cure it or make it go away or give me any real peace. It just gives me something to do while I'm feeling it, if that makes any sense at all. It's just a terrible, endless cycle.

Oh, my goodness, yes. Yes, indeed. This isn't anything new at all, not by a long shot. I've been this way since I was in pigtails, I really have. My poor mother, rest her soul, she used to say I was like a little wind-up toy that someone had wound too tight and just let loose in the house. 

I remember back in grade school—oh, let's see, it must have been Mrs. Gable's third-grade class. Or maybe Mr. Henderson in fourth? No, no, it was definitely Mrs. Gable, she had those thick horn-rimmed glasses and she always smelled faintly of peppermint and chalk dust. Anyway, my mother kept all my old report cards in this big floral shoebox in the attic, and I looked through them a few years ago when I was cleaning out the house. Every single one of those teachers wrote the exact same thing about me, year after year. 

They always wrote that I was a very bright girl, very capable, but just terribly careless. And I was! I was always, always losing my papers. I would sit at the kitchen table and do my arithmetic homework, I swear I would, but by the time I walked to school and sat down at my desk, the paper had just vanished into thin air. It drove my parents up the wall. 

And the talking! Oh, I was quite the chatterbox, always talking out of turn. Mrs. Gable was constantly having to hush me because I'd just blurt things out before she even finished asking the question, or I'd be whispering to the girl next to me about what we were going to play at recess. And she was always, always having to give me reminders just to stay in my seat. I'd be up at the pencil sharpener, or walking over to look at the class hamster, or just standing up at my desk for no good reason at all. I just couldn't stay put. 

And finishing my work? Well, that was a whole other battle. I'd start a spelling worksheet with all the enthusiasm in the world, get halfway through, and then my mind would just be off to the races about something else entirely. I'd start doodling in the margins, and the teacher would have to come tap on my desk and remind me to actually finish what I was doing. 

So, yes, to answer your question, this isn't just something that popped up in my old age or after Frank passed. It's been the story of my whole life. I honestly thought maybe I'd outgrow it, you know? People always say you settle down and get more sedate when you get older, but here I am at sixty-six, and I'm still that same little girl bouncing out of her chair and leaving half-finished projects all over the house!

Losing things? You know, nowadays... not really. I mean, I know I just told you a minute ago that I was always losing my homework when I was a little girl, but these days, I really don't struggle with that very much at all. Because they're on the chain, they are always right here on my chest, so I can't possibly misplace them.

I might move them around a lot—like I was saying earlier about how I'm always pacing and picking things up and putting them down—but I don't actually lose them. I might carry the television remote into the kitchen and set it on top of the microwave while I'm wiping the counters, but I know it's on the microwave because I just put it there! So I don't really have that problem of things just vanishing on me anymore. I keep a pretty tight ship when it comes to knowing where my things are.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Oh, heavens, yes. Yes, I am. Sidetracked is exactly the word for it. It's a terrible thing, really, how easily my mind just wanders off. 

Just the other day—I think it was Tuesday, because Tuesday is usually the day the mail carrier, Tom, drops off the heavier mail. He's such a nice young man, always makes sure the magazines don't get bent. Anyway, I was sitting at the kitchen table, trying to sort through my bills and paperwork. I have this little system, a green folder for the utilities and a red one for anything medical, but getting myself to actually sit there and focus on sorting them is just a monumental chore. 

So, I'm sitting there, I've got my reading glasses on—the ones on the beaded chain I told you about—and I'm finally trying to look at the electric bill. And then, out on the street, I hear a car door shut. Just a normal, everyday sound, right? But I just have to look. I get up, look out the window, and it's just Mrs. Higgins from next door coming home from the grocery store. But by the time I turn back to the table, my brain has completely lost its place. 

And it's not just noises outside. If my cell phone lights up—it doesn't even have to ring, mind you, just light up silently with one of those silly notifications, maybe an email from that craft store I like—that's it. My attention is completely hijacked. I'll stare at the screen and completely forget what I was doing with the paperwork. 

Sometimes it doesn't even take anything happening in the room! I could just be sitting there, staring right at the water bill, and suddenly a thought will just pop into my head about the garden. I'll think, "Oh, I wonder if the hydrangeas need pruning?" Frank planted those hydrangeas the year before he passed, beautiful big blue ones. They need a very specific acidic soil, you know, you have to put coffee grounds in the dirt to keep them that lovely blue color or they turn pink. And before I even realize what's happening, I've left the bills on the kitchen table, walked out the back door, and I'm standing in the yard inspecting the bushes! 

It just pulls me completely off track. I'll find those papers sitting there three hours later and wonder where on earth the afternoon went. It's like my attention is just a little leaf blowing in the wind, going whichever way the breeze takes it, no matter how hard I try to just sit and finish my tasks.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Oh, it’s a daily struggle, it really is. I forget just the most ordinary, everyday things, over and over again, to the point where it’s frankly a little embarrassing. 

Take my daughter, Emily, for instance. She’ll call me—usually in the morning when I’m trying to make my oatmeal. I like the steel-cut kind, you know, because it has a much better texture than the instant, but you really have to stand there and stir it or it sticks to the bottom of the pot. Anyway, she’ll call, and I’ll say, "Honey, let me just take this off the burner and I will call you right back." And then? Poof. Completely gone from my mind. I'll go about my day, maybe water the plants or start a load of towels, and she’ll call me three hours later, absolutely exasperated, asking why I never called her back. And I just feel terrible because I didn't mean to ignore her, I just completely forgot!

And it’s the exact same thing with those bills I was just telling you about. I have my little green and red folder system, which is wonderful in theory, but actually remembering to pay the bill once I've sorted it? That’s another story entirely. I’ll leave a bill sitting right there on the table, fully intending to write the check after lunch, and I just forget it exists. I won't remember it again until two weeks later when I get one of those awful, glaring red notices in the mail saying my account is past due! It makes me feel so foolish, like I can’t even manage my own affairs, even though I have the money sitting right there in the checking account. 

And just last week—oh, this was so frustrating—I had a meeting with the ladies at the church. We’re planning the spring rummage sale, and I had promised faithfully to bring this specific blue folder that had all our volunteer sign-up sheets from last year. I even set it on the little console table right under that horseshoe key hook I told you about, thinking to myself, "You can’t possibly miss this on your way out." Well, wouldn't you know it, I walked right out the front door, drove all the way to the parish hall, sat down with my styrofoam cup of decaf, and realized I had completely forgotten the folder. I had to get up and drive all the way back home to get it while everyone else waited. It’s just... it’s exhausting, always forgetting these simple little things, day in and day out, no matter how hard I try to remind myself.

Oh, it's dreadful, just dreadful. I used to be such a reader, you know. Back in my thirties, I could sit and devour a whole mystery novel in a single afternoon. But nowadays? It’s nearly impossible to keep my mind on anything for more than a few minutes. 

Take the senior center newsletter, for example. I nod and I smile, and I look her right in the eye, but halfway through, my brain just sort of... unplugs. I'll realize I haven't actually absorbed a single word she's said for the last five minutes. I have to just politely smile and hope she didn't just ask me a question. It takes so much energy just to try and force myself to follow along, and even then, I just can't seem to hold my focus on it.

Oh, the grocery store, the pharmacy, the post office... anywhere there is a line, it is just agonizing for me. I get so incredibly edgy, like my skin is suddenly too tight or there's this motor humming inside my chest that just won't let me be still. 

Take the clinic desk, for instance. Not your lovely receptionist, of course, but over at Dr. Evans' office, my podiatrist. They put in this new computer system last fall, and the line just creeps along. If I'm standing there and the person ahead of me is taking forever—maybe they're digging through their bottomless purse for an insurance card or asking a dozen questions about their copay—I just can't bear it. I catch myself huffing and sighing out loud, shifting my weight from foot to foot, just practically vibrating. And before I even realize what I'm doing, I'll catch myself stepping right up to the counter and speaking, trying to just hurry the whole thing along, even if the poor person ahead of me hasn't even finished their transaction! 

And it's not just in formal lines, either. It happens all the time after choir practice. Like I mentioned, David is our director, and he's wonderful, but after we finish rehearsing the anthems, everyone always wants a piece of his time. If I need to ask him a quick question about the sheet music, or even if I just want to say goodnight and head out to my car, and someone else is already talking to him... well, I just don't have the patience to stand there and wait my turn. I'll just step right in. I'll start speaking right over them before they are even finished with their sentence! 

I always feel terrible afterward because I know it comes across as terribly rude, and I certainly wasn't raised to interrupt people like that, but the waiting just makes me so jittery and wound up. It's like the words just push their way out of my mouth because I simply cannot stand there and wait another second.

Do I often have trouble finishing things? Oh, my goodness, yes. Yes, I do. It's actually quite embarrassing, especially when other people are depending on me. And it's not that I don't want to do the things, or that I don't understand what needs to be done... it's just that I get so easily sidetracked!

Take the quilting charity I volunteer for, for instance. We make these beautiful little lap quilts for the veterans' hospital over in the next county. It's a wonderful program, and I've been doing it for, oh, let's see... it must be five years now. Anyway, the coordinator, Susan—she's a lovely woman, very organized, used to be a school principal, I think—she'll give me a list of three or four things to do. She'll say, "Margaret, can you cut the batting, press these squares, and then bind the edges on that blue one?" 

And I always start off so well! I'll take the list, I'll get my good fabric scissors out—the heavy ones, not the ones I use for paper, of course—and I'll start cutting the batting right away. I'm very eager to help. But then, while I'm cutting, I might notice that the ironing board cover is getting a little loose, so I'll stop to fix that. And while I'm fixing the ironing board, I'll remember that I need to water the African violets on the windowsill right above it. And before you know it, I'm in the kitchen looking for my watering can, and I notice the dishwasher needs emptying, and... well, you see where this is going. 

I'll just wander from one chore to another, completely forgetting what I was supposed to be doing in the first place. And poor Susan's quilting tasks... well, the batting might get cut, but the squares never get pressed, and those blue edges certainly never get bound. The last steps just never get done. I always end up having to apologize and take the pieces home with me to finish, which just makes me feel terrible because I know Susan relies on us to get these things done during our meeting time. But I just can't seem to follow through once I get started on something else!

Oh, sitting still? Heavens, it’s nearly impossible for me. It really is. You’d think at my age I could just learn to sit quietly, but no, my body just refuses to cooperate! 

Take our Wednesday morning church meetings, for example. We meet in the fellowship hall—not the main sanctuary, but the hall in the basement where they have those metal folding chairs. They have a little bit of tan padding on the seats, but they aren't the most comfortable things in the world. But even so, when Pastor Davis is giving the morning devotional, and everyone else is just sitting there listening so peacefully, I just cannot keep my body quiet. 

I’ll be sitting there, and without even realizing I’m doing it at first, I’m tapping my foot on the linoleum. Just tap, tap, tap, away I go.
